newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: Dutch say French polls won't undermine EU summit.
newsitem.headline: Dutch say French polls won't undermine EU summit.

text.p: Snap parliamentary elections in France are unlikely to jeopardise the Dutch EU presidency's chances of rounding off intergovernmental consultations on European Union treaty reform at the Amsterdam summit in June, Dutch Prime Minister Wim Kok said on Wednesday.

"I believe that the political will to come to a total accord on IGC in Amsterdam enjoys broad support in France, both among the ruling and opposition parties," Kok told a briefing of European journalists.
French president Jacques Chirac on Monday dissolved the National Assembly, bringing forward elections by 10 months.

Announcing his decision to send the nation to the polls on May 25 and June 1, Chirac argued France needed a government with a renewed legitimacy to prepare for a single European currency and reform the state, cutting public spending and taxes.

"Despite the complications which may arise from the early elections...I am still counting on the willingness of the 15 member states to round off (the Intergovernmental Conference) with a Treaty of Amsterdam," Kok said.
Kok did not regard the debate in France on EMU as a threat to treaty reform. "Of course there is quite an exchange of views on EMU (in France) but that is more an issue for next year."
Nor would the French elections affect the timing of an informal interim summit meeting of EU heads of government in the southern Dutch town of Maastricht tentatively scheduled for May 23, Kok said.
"We have had no indication from the Elysee (Paris) that the date will pose a problem," he said.

The Dutch presidency is to decide in early May -- after British general elections on May 1 -- whether to go ahead with the informal meeting, seen by many commentators as a bid to bring a new British government on side ahead of the closing Amsterdam summit on June 16 and 17.
The Maastricht meeting would not take any formal decisions but was aimed at reaffirming the political will for an accord on treaty reform, the Dutch premier said.
French elections would simply strengthen the general consultative nature of such a meeting, he said.

Kok added that while a gap of a mere fortnight between the second wave of French elections on June 1 and the Amsterdam summit would not make IGC negotiations any easier, it did not make the chances of success any less likely.
Experience had shown that breakthroughs were often achieved in the very final stages, he said.

Asked whether the decision to go ahead with a meeting in Maastricht -- venue of an earlier landmark treaty establishing the ground rules for a single Europe -- depended on the outcome of the British elections, Kok said it did not.
Instead the Netherlands wished first to gauge the degree of progress booked in ministerial and other negotiating forums this month, he said.
However a decision in favour of an additional informal summit should not be interpreted as a sign of weakness, he said, adding it was more likely to be held than not.
